title: The humble houseplant: an aid for health and cleanliness

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A growing body of research is showing that plants can reduce dust particles and contaminants, such as formaldehyde and benzene, that come from cigarette smoke, paint, building materials and other sources. Big growers such as Costa Farms, based in Florida in the US, and retailers Lowe's and Home Depot, now sell plants with tags promoting the air-cleaning abilities. The advantage of plants as air purifiers is people can sometimes solve their air quality problem with as little as $100 worth of plants, or propagate their own plants, according to Stanley J. Kays, a horticulture professor at the University of Georgia (UGA) in the US, which is spearheading plant research with scientists in South Korea. In addition to studying existing plants, researchers there are trying to see if certain species could be bred to create super-efficient air cleaners.

Kays, a horticulture professor at the University of Georgia (UGA) in the US, which is spearheading plant research with scientists in South Korea. In addition to studying existing plants, researchers there are trying to see if certain species could be bred to create super-efficient air cleaners.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Interest in plants as air purifiers comes amid mounting concerns about the quality of indoor air. People spend more than 90% of their time inside, where levels of a dozen common organic pollutants can be two to five times higher than outside, according to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in the US. Associated health problems range from headaches and asthma to respiratory diseases and cancer. The agency says it is particularly concerned about air quality in homes that have taken steps to be more energy efficient by adding insulation and other techniques that protect against draughts.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: That said, plants aren't yet recognized as a mainstream air filtration tool. The EPA says, 'there is currently no evidence.. that a reasonable number of houseplants can remove significant quantities of pollutants in homes and offices.' The US Green Building Council, which certifies buildings based on environmental standards, says, 'while using plants to help clean air is a great strategy. we've had difficulty quantifying the results.' That could be changing. Studies conducted over the past five years by the University of Technology, Sydney, in Australia found that small groups of the Janet Craig and Sweet Chico plants placed in offices with high airborne concentrations of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) consistently reduced total VOC levels by up to 75%. 'Potted plants can provide an efficient, self-regulating, low-cost, sustainable bio remediation system for indoor air pollution,' researchers concluded. In another study at Washington State University in the US, dust was reduced by as much as 20% when several plants were placed around a computer lab and small office for one week.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Margaret Burchett, the professor who led the Sydney studies, says that six or more plants in a 1,200 to 1,500 squarefoot house could achieve noteworthy contaminant reductions. At work, 'if you have a couple of nice plants sitting on your desk, it will help purify the air you breathe,' says Bill Wolverton, a NASA scientist and author of Plants: Why You Can't Live Without Them.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Indoor-air pollutants come in two primary forms: particle pollutants, such as dust, pollen, and smoke, and gaseous pollutants such as VOCs that are emitted from sources like building materials and aerosol sprays. Plants clean the air, researchers say, by absorbing pollution through small pores called stomata, and via microorganisms in the soil or medium that metabolize contaminants. Scientists believe plants can begin removing pollution the moment they're placed in a room, and can be particularly useful in spaces where theres little ventilation.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Pinpointing specific air quality problems can be tricky. Do-it-yourself kits and environmental companies can conduct air-quality tests at consumers' homes. However, analyzing the results can be confusing because there's no universal standard for acceptable levels of many VOCs, according to the EPA. As for remedies, ventilation often works best, but not every climate is suitable for open windows and doors. Mechanical ventilation units can cost from $600 to upwards of $2,500, not including installation. That's why researchers see opportunity for plants, which are inexpensive and relatively easy to maintain. In 2009, UGA scientists identified five 'super ornamentals' plants that showed an ability to remove high rates of contaminants when exposed to common household VOCs. They are: purple waffle, English ivy, asparagus fern, purple heart plant, and the variegated wax plant. UGA's Dr Kays and his colleagues aim to develop a test kit homeowners can use to check for VOCs, as well as an expanded list of plants and their pollution-fighting abilities. The university also sees a potential market for an enhanced medium for growing plants.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Plants did not feature widely, as the minimalist look in architecture prevailed in recent years, says Mike Lewis, president of the Green Plants for Green Buildings advocacy group. 'Now when you talk to architects.... they want plants back.' When designing the new Henry Ford West Bloomfield Hospital in Michigan in the US, the hospital's CEO Gerard van Grinsven says he placed $150,000 worth of live plants in the facility. 'The plants are doing what they are supposed to do – produce oxygen and filter all these bad elements from our environment,' Mr van Grinsven says.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Wolverton, who continued his plant research after leaving NASA, has helped develop a $199 planter which uses an electric fan and activated carbon in a ceramic growing medium (no earth) to filter and trap pollutants around plants roots more efficiently so microbes can metabolize them. Norman Ankers, a lawyer, says he and his wife have filled their 5,000 squarefoot home with ferns and orchids. 'We don't pretend to understand the complex chemistry of it all,' Ankers says. 'But having something that's a cleaning agent or filter is an extra benefit.'

subtitle: Building on NASA experiments for air purification in space, scientists are pinpointing plant species that are skillful at cleaning indoor air of pollutants that can cause a range of health problems.
